Instant Meshes — vendored source (compute half only)
====================================================

Upstream:  https://github.com/wjakob/instant-meshes
Commit:    7b3160864a2e1025af498c84cfed91cbfb613698
License:   BSD-3-Clause — see LICENSE.txt
Paper:     Jakob, Tarini, Panozzo, Sorkine-Hornung,
           "Instant Field-Aligned Meshes", SIGGRAPH Asia 2015

What is vendored
----------------
`src/` holds the field solve and the mesh extraction — the half of upstream
that computes — **plus this project's patches**, recorded as `review.patch`
(a unified diff against the pristine upstream files, 41 hunks across six).

The viewer, the command-line front end and the mesh I/O are **not** vendored:
`main.cpp`, `batch.cpp`, `viewer.cpp`, `widgets.cpp`, `glutil.cpp`,
`meshio.cpp`, `diff.cpp` and `serializer.cpp` are all absent, and with them the
dependencies on nanogui, OpenGL and rply. `serializer.h` stays because
`MultiResolutionHierarchy` and `Optimizer` declare `save`/`load` against it and
every one of its `set`/`get` overloads is defined inline in the header; nothing
here ever constructs one.

`src/review_support.cpp` is added by this project, not upstream. It defines the
one symbol the trimmed tree references and `main.cpp` used to supply
(`int nprocs`).

`ext/` carries the two single-header dependencies upstream pulls in as git
submodules, so this tree needs none:

  dset.h   https://github.com/wjakob/dset  — lock-free disjoint set
                                             (Zlib; LICENSE.dset.txt)
  pcg32.h  https://github.com/wjakob/pcg32 — PCG random number generator
                                             (Apache-2.0, stated in its own
                                             header; upstream carries no
                                             separate licence file)

`shim/` is entirely this project's:

  tbb/tbb.h              the slice of Intel TBB the compute set uses,
  tbb/concurrent_vector.h  reimplemented over the C++ standard library. It goes
                         on the include path *ahead* of everything else, so the
                         vendored `#include <tbb/...>` lines resolve to it and
                         not one vendored line changes. Its own header explains
                         the determinism and threading contract — including
                         `shim::SerialScope`, which is what makes upstream's
                         `deterministic` flag true rather than nearly true: that
                         flag never reached the field solve, and the field solve
                         is not reproducible across thread counts.
  review_quiet.h         the sink `cout`/`cerr` the one `common.h` hunk names.

`ext/pss` (Intel's parallel stable sort) is deliberately absent: it is used at
two call sites, both on upstream's own `deterministic` path, and both are
patched to `std::stable_sort`. That is what removes the last TBB-shaped
dependency the shim would otherwise have to grow a task scheduler for.

The patches
-----------
P1  `common.h` — `using std::cout` / `using std::cerr` become references to a
    sink stream (`shim/review_quiet.h`). Instant Meshes narrates every stage to
    the console; the viewer has none, and the remesh runs on a worker thread
    whose stdout would interleave with everything else. Written as two `static`
    references rather than a `#define cout`, so `std::cout` still means
    `std::cout` in any header included after this one.

P2  `hierarchy.cpp` — `pss::parallel_stable_sort` becomes `std::stable_sort`.

P3  `extract.cpp` — the same substitution.

P4  `hierarchy.h` / `hierarchy.cpp` — a **per-vertex scale field**
    (`MultiResolutionHierarchy::mS`, `scaleAt`, `setScaleField`). Upstream
    carries one face size for the whole object, `mScale`, which spends the same
    budget on a flat panel as on a tight fillet; `mS` optionally multiplies it
    per vertex so the solve can put small faces where the surface turns. The
    field is supplied for level 0 and averaged down the hierarchy exactly as
    every other per-vertex quantity is.

    It is *optional* on purpose. `scaleAt` answers `mScale` when the field is
    empty, and every site that reads it goes through `scaleAt`, so a run that
    does not ask for a varying face size takes the same arithmetic it always did
    — not an equivalent expression, the same one. `crates/optimize`'s
    `remesh::RemeshParams::adaptive_strength` at 0 is what leaves it empty, and
    `src/remesh_density.cpp` is what fills it otherwise.

P5  `field.h` / `field.cpp` — the eight `compat_position_*` functions take one
    scale per *endpoint* (`scale0, inv_scale0, scale1, inv_scale1`) instead of
    one for the pair, and the four sites that call them — the position solve,
    its error measure, the position singularities and the integer-variable
    freeze — read each vertex's own. This is the change P4 exists for: without
    it the hierarchy could carry a field nothing would consult. It is the same
    shape QuadriFlow's fork of this code took for the same reason, which is
    where the treatment of the anchored lattice in the intrinsic variants comes
    from.

    With equal scales every one of these reduces to upstream's arithmetic term
    for term. The single exception is the frozen branch of the position solve,
    where `scale * (a - b)` becomes `scale_j * a - scale_i * b`: algebraically
    the same, not bit-identical, and unreachable from this project — the
    integer variables are frozen after the solve, never during it.

P6  `extract.cpp` — the extraction honours the scale field where it decides
    *geometry*, and is bounded where it loops.

    `extract_graph` gives each extracted vertex the face size it came out of
    (`scale_new`, averaged over the same cluster as its position), and the edge
    classification measures each endpoint against its own. The snapping pass
    then uses that per-vertex size rather than one for the object. That is not a
    refinement: with a single threshold, a region the field made fine has *every*
    edge under it, and the pass — whose exit condition is "nothing moved", and
    one of whose branches moves a vertex without removing anything — flattens
    that region a step at a time without ever settling. Measured, before this: a
    sculpted pedestal at half strength never came back. The same loop also gains
    a pass ceiling, because a loop with no other bound is one bad mesh away from
    hanging the viewer.

    The two thresholds that are *heuristics over the whole object* rather than
    lattice arithmetic — the vertex-snapping weight's falloff and the ray length
    in the hole-filling check — stay on the uniform scale.

Refreshing this directory is therefore: copy the newer upstream `src/` files
in, update the commit above, re-apply `review.patch` (`git apply
third_party/instant-meshes/review.patch`, resolving any drift by hand),
regenerate the patch from the result, then re-run `crates/optimize`'s `remesh`
and `export_round_trip` suites. P4–P6 are a fork of the solver rather than a
substitution, so a refresh has to be read rather than applied: the three tests
that pin them are `varying_face_size_spends_the_budget_on_the_curved_parts`,
`the_face_count_is_the_one_that_was_asked_for` and
`a_varied_rebuild_is_reproducible`. If the refresh reaches for a TBB facility the
shim has no entry for, that is a compile error naming it — never a silent
behaviour change.

How it is built
---------------
`crates/optimize/build.rs` compiles this alongside `src/remesh_bridge.cpp` with
`cc`, gated on **both** this directory and `third_party/eigen`, and sets
`cfg(has_instant_meshes)` only when both are present — the same
optional-vendoring contract `crates/import` has for ufbx. Delete either and the
workspace still builds; the Remesh operation then reports
`OptError::RemeshUnavailable` as a per-operation warning and every other
operation still runs.

It is compiled at `opt_level(2)` in **every** profile, with `NDEBUG` and
`EIGEN_NO_DEBUG`. Eigen's expression templates collapse to nothing at `-O2` and
to a tower of tiny calls at `-O0`; an unoptimized build turns a
hundred-thousand-triangle remesh from seconds into minutes, which `cargo test`
would pay on every run.
